entities.description: 1 Ashwin, nine nights. This entity covers Sharad Navratri, the autumn observance leading into Dussehra/Vijayadashami — the larger and more widely observed of the two annual Navratri periods (the other, Chaitra Navratri, falls in spring and shares the same nine-form structure). Each of the nine nights is dedicated to one form of the Navadurga, the nine aspects of Durga, in a fixed traditional sequence drawn from the Devi Bhagavata Purana.

dayCorrespondences.label: Night 1 — Shailputri
dayCorrespondences.description: "Daughter of the Mountain" — Durga as Parvati, the form invoked on the opening night.

dayCorrespondences.label: Night 2 — Brahmacharini
dayCorrespondences.description: The ascetic form, embodying penance and unwavering devotion.

dayCorrespondences.label: Night 3 — Chandraghanta
dayCorrespondences.description: "Bearer of the crescent-bell," a fierce, war-ready form worn for courage.

dayCorrespondences.label: Night 4 — Kushmanda
dayCorrespondences.description: Said to have created the universe with a smile; associated with the sun's inner radiance.

dayCorrespondences.label: Night 5 — Skandamata
dayCorrespondences.description: Mother of Skanda (Kartikeya), invoked for maternal protection.

dayCorrespondences.label: Night 6 — Katyayani
dayCorrespondences.description: The warrior form born to sage Katyayana, later identified with Durga's slaying of Mahishasura.

dayCorrespondences.label: Night 7 — Kalaratri
dayCorrespondences.description: "Night of death," the fiercest and darkest form, invoked against fear itself.

dayCorrespondences.label: Night 8 — Mahagauri
dayCorrespondences.description: The radiant, purified form, associated with compassion and calm.

dayCorrespondences.label: Night 9 — Siddhidatri
dayCorrespondences.description: "Giver of siddhis," bestowing spiritual accomplishment; the culminating form before Vijayadashami.

entities.description: The 14th tithi of Phalguna's dark fortnight — approximated here as the second-to-last civil day of the native Hindu month, immediately preceding the new moon that closes it. "The Great Night of Shiva" is kept with an all-night vigil (jagarana), fasting, and continuous worship at Shiva lingams, commemorating the night Shiva is said to have performed the cosmic dance of creation, preservation, and destruction (Tandava), and, in some traditions, the night of his marriage to Parvati.
